p: Ulugh Khan was originally named Almas Beg. His father, Shihabuddin Mas'ud, was the elder brother of Sultan Jalaluddin, founder of the Khalji dynasty, and both Almas Beg and his elder brother Alauddin married daughters of Jalaluddin. Under Jalaluddin he held the post of Akhur-beg, equivalent to master of the horse. In 1296, after Alauddin had raided Devagiri and kept the loot, Almas Beg assured the sultan of his brother's loyalty and persuaded him to visit Kara, where Alauddin killed him on 20 July 1296. The new sultan made his brother barbeg with the title Ulugh Khan, meaning Great Khan. He also held the iqta' of Bayana.

In November 1296 Alauddin sent him and Zafar Khan with an army of 30,000 to 40,000 against Multan, held by Jalaluddin's son Arkali Khan. After two months of siege the leaders of the defence went over to Delhi. Ulugh Khan promised Arkali Khan and his brother Ruknuddin Ibrahim that they would not be harmed, but imprisoned them once the city was occupied; they were later blinded or killed by Nusrat Khan on Alauddin's orders. According to the courtier Amir Khusrau, he reached the Sutlej River on 6 February 1298 and defeated the Mongols of the Chagatai Khanate there, with 20,000 Mongol dead.

On the way back from Gujarat in 1299, near Jalore, he and Nusrat Khan punished soldiers for withholding the khums, the fifth of the loot due to the treasury. Recently converted Mongol soldiers mutinied; some 2,000 to 3,000 attacked his camp and killed a nephew of Alauddin whom they took for him. Against Hammira of Ranthambore in 1301 he defeated and killed the general Bhimasimha at the Banas River, but after Nusrat Khan was killed in the siege he was forced back to Jhain, and Alauddin came in person and took the fort in July 1301.

Ordered to prepare a march on the Kakatiya capital Warangal, he assembled a large army but died a few months later. The chronicler Ziauddin Barani writes that Alauddin was greatly depressed and gave much in charity for his brother's soul. Barani's contemporary Isami claims instead that Alauddin had him poisoned, suspecting that he had been ready to take the throne when the sultan was wrongly reported dead; later chroniclers repeat this. The historian Banarsi Prasad Saksena dismisses Isami's account as false, while Kishori Saran Lal thinks it not impossible. Claims that he led the invasion of Gujarat in 1304, or governed it for 20 years, are of doubtful accuracy.

notes: The entry says 'd. 1302'; the article says 'died c. 1302', a few months after July 1301.
The entry says he 'defeated a Mongol invasion in 1298'; the article dates the raid to the winter of 1297 and the battle to 6 February 1298.
Barani's story that Alauddin and Ulugh Khan plotted against Zafar Khan, and Hajiuddabir's that he withheld help at Kili, were left out (the article says historians doubt the first).
The killing of rebels and of Fakhruddin's grandsons at Delhi after Haji Maula's revolt (1301) was left out for room; the editor may want it, as harm done on his orders.
